Where channels agree, a stated plan is a good guide to the action that follows, so it is worth reading. Its correctness still has to be checked against the state, because a consistent action carries an incorrect plan into effect as faithfully as a correct one. Scoring execution length or success rates mostly measures easy states. In debt resolution the consequential decision is whether to stop, and in bargaining it is whether to refuse. Those are the decisions where the stated assessment should be compared with the record.

exact_passage: A record can show five things about a stated consequence. It can be (1) \emph{stated} before the action, (2) \emph{accurate} against the state and rules, (3) \emph{consistent} with the action taken, (4) \emph{sensitive}, meaning behavior changes when the consequence changes, and (5) \emph{effective}, meaning the behavior improves an outcome against a reference. Each result is tagged once with the highest level it reaches. None reaches level five, because the games contain no reference policy or value estimate.
evidence: Accuracy and action consistency are not nested levels. An inaccurate assessment can produce a consistent action.
recommendation: Use dimensions and concrete statements, not highest-level labels.

exact_passage: Counts are exact for this finite cohort. When we describe uncertainty, the target is the difference between two pooled rejection shares for a cohort of the same design: the same roster and configurations, five seed blocks of four rotations. Games within a block share a seed and are not independent draws. Our primary summary therefore resamples seed blocks and then games within each drawn block (20,000 draws); Appendix~\ref{app:offers} adds resampling by games alone and by whole blocks, and every block separately. An earlier draft's authors found the offer-form contrast after inspecting this corpus, so these intervals describe its spread within the cohort and do not confirm it. We report no p-values.

recommendation: Use intact-block resampling as primary descriptive stability; label any other unit as a different perturbation.

exact_passage: Response conditions differ across systems (Table~\ref{tab:config}). An invalid response normally receives one corrective request and then a deterministic fallback. When a provider refuses a first attempt, the second attempt instead uses an action-only prompt with no private note. All 1,605 refusals are of Opus and carry one identical provider message about reproducing model outputs; none of the recovery calls is refused. Opus therefore plays 1,604 of its 1,696 decisions without a note and without a further correction, and the text we read for Opus is its provider-returned reasoning. Grok runs with \texttt{tool\_choice} set to \texttt{required}; the others use \texttt{auto}. In 1,068 selected Grok responses the assistant content names an action, and in 139 that action differs from the call the engine applied. We cannot attribute these conflicts to the tool-choice setting, but other agents answered the offers they produced. Finally, past-trade summaries misattribute some authors or terms in 2,054 prompts; current holdings and every current offer are correct.

exact_passage: \noindent Some moves matter for what they make possible next. We ask whether LLM agents state such consequences before they act, whether the statements are accurate, and whether their actions agree with them, using twenty complete four-player Monopoly games with free-form negotiation among four configured systems (GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5, Grok 4.7). For the agent's own options we examine all \fact{d.episodes} debts that required liquidation. Agents declared bankruptcy at the first menu in \fact{d.above-bound.declared-at-first-menu} of \fact{d.above-bound.episodes} debts that exceeded everything they owned and in \fact{x.debt.payable.declared} of \fact{d.payable} payable debts. Sixteen payable debts could be met only with mortgages that the menu lists after buildings are sold, a rule and values the prompt does not supply. Agents paid fourteen. The text stored before the first action counts the unlisted mortgages in thirteen of those, raises them in one, and omits them in both failures. For a rival's options we examine all \fact{o.census.responses.n} responses to trade offers. Recipients accepted \fact{x.po.accept} of \fact{x.po.n} opening offers that would complete only the proposer's color group. They rejected \fact{x.swpo.rej.pct}\% of such swaps against \fact{x.swn.rej.pct}\% of swaps completing no group, a gap of \fact{o.sensitivity.swap-gap-without-grok-authors.point-pp} to \fact{o.sensitivity.swap-gap.point-pp} points depending on which proposers are counted, and they countered cash bids more often than swaps. Refusals mention the rival's set under both forms, yet rejection does not rise with the building the rival could then afford. Eight sourced incidents place these statements in context, including a deed sold as insurance against a third player's inheritance. Stated foresight about the agent's own financing is accurate and matches action. Stated concern about rivals matches action and attaches to the event of completion. The study is observational, covers one cohort under unequal response conditions, and measures neither effectiveness nor model rank.
evidence: 186 is the swap-plus-cash-bid subset; all acceptance-legal proposer-only openings include one other bundle for 187.
recommendation: Name the two forms next to the aggregate or use the full denominator.
